<h1>Multi-DOF Systems: Coupled Equations & Modal Superposition</h1>
<p class="hero-lead">
Assemble global mass $\mathbf{M}$ and stiffness $\mathbf{K}$ matrices for 
<span class="highlight-blue">discrete mechanical networks</span>. Formulate the 
<span class="highlight-orange">generalized algebraic eigenvalue problem</span>, establish modal orthogonality, 
and uncouple complex coupled differential equations into independent <span class="highlight-teal">normal coordinates</span>.
</p>
</div>

Learning Outcomes

<ul style="margin: 0; padding-left: 20px;">
<li><strong>Assemble</strong> symmetric positive-definite mass and stiffness matrices for multi-storey and multi-body structures.</li>
<li><strong>Solve</strong> the characteristic determinant $\det(\mathbf{K} - \omega^2 \mathbf{M}) = 0$ for natural frequencies and mode shape vectors.</li>
<li><strong>Prove & leverage</strong> mass-orthogonality $\mathbf{\Phi}^T \mathbf{M} \mathbf{\Phi} = \mathbf{I}$ to decouple large coupled systems.</li>
<li><strong>Compute</strong> transient forced responses via modal superposition without inverting coupled differential operators.</li>
</ul>

<!-- Section 2: Theory -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-theory">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">01 · Matrix Formulations</div>
<h2>3.1 Coupled Matrix Equations of Motion</h2>
<p>For an $n$-degree-of-freedom discrete linear structure undergoing small vibrations, dynamic equilibrium in matrix form is written:</p>
</div>

<div class="card">
<div class="eq-box">
$$\mathbf{M} \ddot{\mathbf{x}}(t) + \mathbf{C} \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) + \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{f}(t)$$
</div>

<p>
Where $\mathbf{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is the positive-definite mass matrix, $\mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is the stiffness matrix, and $\mathbf{x}(t) = [x_1(t), \dots, x_n(t)]^T$ is the physical coordinate displacement vector.
</p>
<p>
Assuming synchronous harmonic free vibration $\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{u} e^{i \omega t}$ yields the generalized algebraic eigenvalue problem:
</p>

<div class="eq-box">
$$(\mathbf{K} - \omega^2 \mathbf{M}) \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0} \quad \implies \quad \det(\mathbf{K} - \omega^2 \mathbf{M}) = 0$$
</div>

<p>
The roots of the characteristic polynomial yield $n$ real natural frequencies $\omega_1 \le \omega_2 \le \dots \le \omega_n$ and $n$ orthogonal mode shape eigenvectors $\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_n$.
</p>
</div>
</section>

<!-- Section 3: Modal Decoupling -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-orthogonality">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">02 · Modal Analysis</div>
<h2>3.2 Modal Coordinates & Decoupling</h2>
<p>Transforming from physical coordinates $\mathbf{x}$ to modal coordinates $\mathbf{q}$ via modal matrix $\mathbf{\Phi} = [\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_n]$.</p>
</div>

<div class="card">
<p>Substituting $\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{\Phi} \mathbf{q}(t)$ and premultiplying by $\mathbf{\Phi}^T$:</p>

<div class="eq-box">
$$\mathbf{\Phi}^T \mathbf{M} \mathbf{\Phi} \ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{\Phi}^T \mathbf{K} \mathbf{\Phi} \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{\Phi}^T \mathbf{f}(t)$$
</div>

<p>By virtue of mass-normalization ($\mathbf{\Phi}^T \mathbf{M} \mathbf{\Phi} = \mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{\Phi}^T \mathbf{K} \mathbf{\Phi} = \operatorname{diag}(\omega_1^2, \dots, \omega_n^2)$), the coupled system separates into $n$ completely independent 1-DOF single-degree modal oscillators:</p>

<div class="eq-box">
$$\ddot{q}_r(t) + \omega_r^2 q_r(t) = Q_r(t) \equiv \mathbf{u}_r^T \mathbf{f}(t), \quad r = 1, \dots, n$$
</div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- Section 4: Misconceptions -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-misconceptions">
<div class="callout-important">
<div class="callout-title">
<svg width="20" height="20" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><path d="M10.29 3.86L1.82 18a2 2 0 0 0 1.71 3h16.94a2 2 0 0 0 1.71-3L13.71 3.86a2 2 0 0 0-3.42 0z"/><line x1="12" y1="9" x2="12" y2="13"/><line x1="12" y1="17" x2="12.01" y2="17"/></svg>
Common Misconception · Do Mode Shapes Represent Absolute Amplitudes?
</div>
<p style="margin: 0 0 8px 0;">
Students often confuse mode shape eigenvectors $\mathbf{u}_r$ with actual physical displacement magnitudes.
</p>
<p style="margin: 0;">
<strong>Mode shapes indicate relative shape ratios only, not absolute displacement units.</strong> An eigenvector can be scaled by any arbitrary constant ($\alpha \mathbf{u}_r$) and still satisfy $(\mathbf{K} - \omega_r^2 \mathbf{M}) \mathbf{u}_r = \mathbf{0}$. Absolute physical displacement is determined only after combining mode shapes with initial conditions and external force amplitudes through modal participation factors!
</p>
</div>
</section>

<!-- Section 5: Quiz -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-quiz">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">03 · Diagnostic Checkpoint</div>
<h2>3.3 Check Your Understanding</h2>
<p>Test your understanding of multi-DOF dynamics and modal decoupling.</p>
</div>

<div class="quiz-box">
<div class="quiz-question">
<strong>Question:</strong> In an undamped 2-DOF mass-spring system, what occurs if an external harmonic force is applied whose spatial distribution is orthogonal to the second mode shape ($\mathbf{u}_2^T \mathbf{f}_0 = 0$)?
</div>
<div class="quiz-options">
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="false" data-explanation="Modal decoupling means modes operate independently. Zero modal force in mode 2 prevents mode 2 from ever receiving energy!">
A. Both modes resonate simultaneously.
</div>
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="true" data-explanation="Since the modal force Q2 = u2^T * f = 0, the second modal coordinate q2(t) receives zero excitation. The structure responds exclusively in mode 1, even if the excitation frequency is tuned close to omega_2!">
B. Mode 2 is never excited (its modal response $q_2(t) = 0$), and the structure oscillates purely in Mode 1.
</div>
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="false" data-explanation="Orthogonality does not create instability; it completely decouples energy transmission!">
C. The system becomes unstable due to anti-resonance.
</div>
</div>
<div class="quiz-feedback"></div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- Section 6: Code -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-code">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">04 · Computational Implementation</div>
<h2>3.4 Generalized Eigenvalue Solution in Python & MATLAB</h2>
<p>Solve for natural frequencies and normalized mode shapes of a 3-DOF shear building structure.</p>
</div>

<div class="code-box">
<div class="code-header">
<div class="code-tabs">
<button class="code-tab-btn active">Python (SciPy eigh)</button>
<button class="code-tab-btn">MATLAB (eig)</button>
</div>
<button class="btn-copy">Copy Code</button>
</div>
<pre class="code-block"><code>import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import eigh

# 3-DOF Mass & Stiffness Matrices
M = np.diag([20.0, 15.0, 10.0]) # Mass matrix (kg)
k1, k2, k3 = 10000.0, 8000.0, 5000.0
K = np.array([
    [k1 + k2,   -k2,         0.0],
    [-k2,       k2 + k3,     -k3],
    [0.0,       -k3,         k3 ]
])

# Solve Generalized Eigenvalue Problem: K * v = w^2 * M * v
eigenvalues, Phi = eigh(K, M)
natural_freqs_hz = np.sqrt(eigenvalues) / (2 * np.pi)

print("Natural Frequencies (Hz):", np.round(natural_freqs_hz, 2))
print("Mass-Normalized Mode Shapes Matrix Phi:\n", np.round(Phi, 3))</code></pre>
<pre class="code-block" hidden><code>% MATLAB Generalized Eigenvalue Solution
M = diag([20, 15, 10]);
K = [18000 -8000 0; -8000 13000 -5000; 0 -5000 5000];

[Phi, D] = eig(K, M);
omega = sqrt(diag(D));
freq_hz = omega / (2*pi);

disp('Frequencies (Hz):'); disp(freq_hz);
disp('Mode Shapes:'); disp(Phi);</code></pre>
</div>
</section>
